content.text:
The feeling that your bladder **doesn’t empty completely** is often called **urinary retention** or **incomplete bladder emptying**. It can happen for several reasons, usually from either **a blockage**, **weak bladder muscle**, or **nerve/signal problems**. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention/symptoms-causes?utm_source=openai))

Common causes include:

- **Enlarged prostate** in men, which can narrow the urine channel and slow or block flow. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/benign-prostatic-hyperplasia/symptoms-causes/syc-20370087?p=1&utm_source=openai))
- **Urinary tract infection (UTI)** or inflammation, which can make urination difficult or cause the sensation you still need to go.
- **Constipation**, because a full rectum can press on the bladder/urethra and affect bladder nerves.
- **Medications**, especially some antihistamines, decongestants, antidepressants, muscle relaxers, opioids, and bladder-control medicines.
- **Nerve problems**, such as from diabetes, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, spinal injury, stroke, or pelvic surgery. ([merckmanuals.com](https://www.merckmanuals.com/en-pr/home/quick-facts-kidney-and-urinary-tract-disorders/disorders-of-urination/urinary-retention?utm_source=openai))
- **Urethral narrowing/stricture**, bladder stones, tumors, or scar tissue.
- **Pelvic organ prolapse** in women, where the bladder/uterus/rectum shifts and affects emptying.
- **Weak or underactive bladder muscle**, sometimes from aging, nerve issues, or long-term overdistension.
- **Recent anesthesia or surgery**, which can temporarily make it hard to urinate.

**Seek urgent medical care now** if you **cannot urinate at all**, have a painful swollen lower belly, fever/chills, back/flank pain, vomiting, new leg weakness/numbness, or blood clots in the urine. Acute urinary retention can become serious and may require catheter drainage. ([niddk.nih.gov](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-retention.?utm_source=openai))

If it’s ongoing but not an emergency, it’s worth seeing a clinician/urologist. They may check a urine test, kidney function, prostate/pelvic exam, and a bladder scan after you pee to measure how much urine is left.
